s: A walled red-light district built by colonial decree
w: Bousbir was a walled-off brothel quarter built into Casablanca under the French protectorate, on the orders of Resident General Lyautey: colonial urban planning applied to vice, segregated behind its own walls and gate. The name has outlived the institution, now shorthand for a stranger footnote of the city's colonial-era planning.

s: Casablanca's working lighthouse at the port's edge
w: El Hank Lighthouse marks the westernmost tip of Casablanca's port, still operated by the country's Port and Maritime Authority, a working aid to navigation rather than a museum piece, standing sentinel where the city's harbour meets the open Atlantic.

s: A Franciscan church turned refuge turned culture house
w: Sultan Hassan I granted this patch of the Medina to the King of Spain in the 1880s, and Franciscans built a church on it around 1890, for decades the seat of the Spanish church in Casablanca. It stopped holding Mass in 1968 and quietly became housing for families in need, before the city reopened it as a cultural centre around 2016.

s: F1 raced here in 1958; McDonald's landed here in 1992
w: Casablanca's fashionable Corniche has pulled off two unlikely firsts: an F1 World Championship round in 1958, and the first McDonald's in Africa and the Arab world in 1992. Beyond the trivia, it's beach clubs along Lalla Meryem and Ain Diab beaches, with the fortified island of Sidi Abderrahman just offshore.

Everyone in Casablanca knows it as the Sony Building, after the sign that once crowned it, but its real name is the IMCAMA, an Albert Greslin Art Deco design from 1928, standing at the junction of Lorraine Boulevard and Agadir Street with the Arab League Park spread out in front. Colonial-era modernism wearing a nickname nobody corrects.

n: School of Fine Arts of Casablanca
s: Birthplace of the 1960s Casablanca School art movement
q: School of Fine Arts of Casablanca casablanca
w: Founded in 1919, this fine arts school became something more consequential in the 1960s, when faculty members Farid Belkahia, Mohamed Melehi and Mohamed Chabaa turned it into the birthplace of the Casablanca School, the modernist movement that broke with colonial-era academic painting and reimagined Moroccan visual identity.
